Subject: Follow-up & next steps — ACME discovery (observability + hyperscaler comparison)

Hi John / Sara —

Thanks again for taking time today. Quick recap from our call and proposed next steps so we can get ACME the artifacts you asked for:

Recap (short):
- Primary goals: reduce inference cost per request, maintain sub-200ms p95 latency for interactive use, and have enterprise-grade observability across models and routes.
- Current constraints: internal infra is on GCP with a mix of batch and real-time traffic; procurement asks for clear TCO comps vs managed hyperscaler endpoints.
- Biggest open questions: how Redwood’s observability (tracing/dashboards/alerting) compares to hyperscalers, and which tests would prove latency/cost claims for your workload.

Requested follow-ups from Redwood:
1) One-pager comparison vs hyperscaler endpoints (latency patterns, cost levers, fallbacks) — attached.
2) Suggested test plan for parity/benchmarks (small set of sample prompts, concurrency targets) — I’m attaching a starter test plan (ACME can tweak).
3) Short demo of our Console observability focused on model-level traces and per-route cost breakdowns — happy to set up next week.

Proposed next steps:
- Dev / Michael: can you review the attached test plan and confirm the probes (concurrency, sequence lengths) match ACME's expected mix?
- John / Sara: if you can share a short representative prompt set and an anonymized traffic profile, we’ll run a 48hr comparative run and share results.

I’ve attached: redwood-vs-hyperscalers-one-pager.pdf and acme-requested-test-plan.xlsx.

Availability: I’m free Wed/Thu mornings next week for the console walkthrough.

Thanks —
Marissa

Marissa —

Thanks for the clear recap and the materials, review underway. A few quick clarifications from our side:

1) Test plan: the concurrency mix in production is spiky (baseline 50rps, occasional bursts to 450rps). We care most about p95 during bursts — do you suggest any specific batching config for that pattern?
2) Observability: our infra team wants to see per-request traces tied to model version and route (so we can correlate quality regressions with deployments). Can Redwood’s Console provide trace sampling at that granularity and export spans to our Elastic stack?
3) Pricing: procurement asked for a 6-month reserved capacity quote vs pay-as-you-go hyperscaler spend example — can you provide a template for the price comparison?

We’ll anonymize a small prompt set and the traffic histogram and share by EOD Friday. Also looping in procurement for the pricing ask.

—John

Subject: RE: Follow-up & next steps — ACME discovery (observability + hyperscaler comparison)

Marissa —

Quick internal note based on John’s replies and the test profile they’ll share:

Notes / recommendations:
- Batching: for spiky burst profiles I recommend starting with an adaptive batching policy: target max latency 180ms p95, dynamic batch cap at 64 tokens/req and a max batch window of 12ms. This preserves tail while giving throughput benefits during microbursts.
- KV cache / prefix caching: if ACME has repeated prefixes (system prompts) we can show 20–40% token savings in early runs. We should ask for a sample of the most common prefixes.
- Observability: Console supports per-request traces with model-version and route tags. We can export spans to Elastic via OTLP; need to confirm sampling rate. For the demo, I can prepare a trace view that maps span attributes to our per-route cost breakdown.
- Tests to run: 48hr run with 3 phases: ramp (24h low), burst injection (12h with synthetic bursts to 450rps), steady (12h at baseline 50rps). Collect p50/p95/p99 latency, tokens/second, cost-per-1000-requests.

Attached to you: a quick internal checklist for the run and a sample Grafana/Elastic export config. I’ll own the run if ACME shares the prompt set and anonymized histogram.

—Dev
Principal Solutions Engineer | Redwood Inference
dev.patel@redwood.com
